blocks.text: The metallic character of an element is its tendency to lose electrons. Elements on the left side of the periodic table have a greater tendency to lose their outermost electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration, while elements on the right tend to gain electrons. So elements on the left are metals that form positive ions, and elements on the right, particularly in the right corner, are non-metals that form negative ions; the metallic character of an element depends largely on its valence shell electronic configuration.

Across a period from left to right the nuclear charge increases and the atomic size decreases, which pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus and makes it harder for the atom to lose electrons, so the metallic character decreases. Down a group the metallic character increases, because the atomic size and the shielding effect increase and reduce the nuclear attraction on the valence electrons. The increase in metallic character, the ease of losing an electron, makes the element more reactive: cesium is far more reactive and electropositive than sodium or lithium.

blocks.caption: Metallic and non-metallic character
rows: Across a period, left to right
Nuclear charge up, size down: electrons held harder
Size and shielding up: valence electrons lost more easily

blocks.prompt: Illustrate how metallic character varies in group 14, and say why silicon and germanium are semimetals.
blocks.explanation: Group 14 runs from carbon, a non-metal, through silicon and germanium, the metalloids, to tin and lead, which are metals: metallic character increases down the group as the atoms grow and the valence electrons are better shielded. Silicon and germanium lie on the stair-step line between metals and non-metals and show some properties of each, so they are semimetals.

items: Metallic character is the tendency to lose electrons; it depends on the valence shell configuration.
It decreases across a period and increases down a group, so reactivity grows down the metals' groups: cesium is far more reactive than sodium or lithium.
